hook_text: This equation has infinitely many answers — and you can write ALL of them in one line.
clip_script: A taxi runs a fixed loop through the neighbourhood, and you see it pass the school gate at eight in the morning. The loop takes exactly one hour. So when else does it pass? Nine. Ten. Eleven. And — think backwards — seven, and six. One sighting plus the loop time gives you the entire timetable, past and future: eight o'clock plus k hours, where k is any whole number. Now here's the secret: that IS trigonometry. Solve sine x equals zero comma eight. The calculator gives you one sighting: fifty-three comma one three degrees. But the wheel repeats every three hundred and sixty degrees — that's the loop. So fifty-three comma one three plus k times three sixty catches every answer that will ever exist. The k isn't scary algebra. It's a lap counter. Rewind a lap, fast-forward a lap. One more twist: within each loop, sine hits most heights TWICE — once riding up, once riding down. So there's a second door: one eighty minus fifty-three comma one three. Two families, each with its own lap counter, and the infinite answer fits on one line. The calculator answers once. The quadrants double it. The loop multiplies it forever.
visual_style: A minibus taxi orbiting a looped road past a glowing school gate, clock faces stamping each pass, then the road morphing into a spinning wheel with degree markings and two doors lighting up on opposite sides.
mood: Aha-energy — an infinite problem folding into one neat line.
pacing: Steady laps to start, snap cuts on each timetable stamp, a slow zoom on the final one-line answer.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and write timetables for the infinite.
